title: Adobe MAX 2026: Adobe Express Is Coming to Microsoft Photos
summary: Adobe MAX announces Adobe Express integration coming directly into Microsoft Photos
detailed: Adobe Express is coming to the Photos app in Windows 11: Windows Insiders will be able to test the integration as a preview starting in December 2026.
Adobe announced this on November 10 at Adobe MAX in Miami Beach.

sentences: Adobe Express is coming to the Photos app in Windows 11: Windows Insiders will be able to test the integration as a preview starting in December 2026.
Adobe announced this on November 10 at Adobe MAX in Miami Beach.

At the same time, optimized versions of Photoshop, Premiere, After Effects, and Substance 3D Painter (beta) are now available for high-performance Windows PCs with Arm chips, particularly for devices with NVIDIA’s RTX Spark, such as the Surface Laptop Ultra.
For most Windows users, the Photos app is where they open and do quick edits on their images.
That’s exactly where Adobe comes in.
Instead of having to launch a separate program first, Adobe-powered AI editing and Express templates will be available directly within Photos.

According to Adobe, this includes:
There’s also a link to Adobe Express itself: From within the photo viewer, you can open an image in Express and preview it in a personalized template—such as for an invitation or a social media post.
You can then continue designing there.
Adobe’s own blog post isn’t entirely clear on the timeline.

The introduction mentions an Insider preview “starting in December,” while further down, regarding the AI tools and templates, it simply says “in the coming months.” It’s quite possible that the features will roll out gradually in the preview.
Neither Adobe nor Microsoft has announced a release date for the final version for all Windows 11 users.
The second part of the announcement is aimed at professionals.
Adobe has optimized its Pro apps for high-performance Arm-based Windows PCs.
According to Adobe, the optimized versions are available now, with Substance 3D Painter currently in beta.
Adobe explicitly cites NVIDIA’s RTX Spark platform as the foundation.

Adobe doesn’t provide specific figures in the MAX post; it only mentions that things are “faster.” However, back in mid-October, Adobe and Nvidia had already stated that the optimized apps on RTX Spark run up to twice as fast for AI processing, editing, color correction, and effects.
This is a manufacturer’s claim.
Independent measurements using the new versions are still pending.
A quick side note for anyone who hasn’t been paying attention lately: Adobe now refers to the desktop app simply as “Premiere”—the “Pro” has been dropped.
The fact that Adobe is pushing Windows on Arm so aggressively right now has to do with Nvidia.
The RTX Spark platform combines an Arm CPU with a Blackwell GPU on a single chip and shares the RAM between the two.
The first devices have been available in stores since October 16, 2026.

In addition to Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra—which recently received a major firmware update —other options include the Dell XPS 16 Creator Edition and the MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI+ as a convertible.
For those who don’t need a laptop, RTX Spark is also available in mini PCs such as the Gigabyte AI TOP AERO, which features up to 128 GB of unified memory.
With the Surface Laptop Ultra, you should pay close attention to the configuration.
The entry-level model, priced at 2,899 euros, uses the smaller RTX Spark configuration with 18 CPU cores, 24 GB of RAM, and a 512 GB SSD.
The full-featured chip with 20 CPU cores and 6,144 CUDA cores starts at 4,239 euros, while the top-of-the-line model with 128 GB of RAM costs 6,879 euros.
You can find more details on Microsoft’s Surface page and in Nvidia’s technical specifications.
You can search for the Surface Laptop Ultra on Amazon.

As concrete as the feature list sounds, Adobe leaves a few important points unaddressed:
Adobe MAX runs through November 12 in Miami Beach and online.
Microsoft has its own “Creator Studio” (Booth 902) where it’s showcasing live demos on Surface devices.
James Howell, Vice President of Windows Consumer Marketing at Microsoft, summarizes the partnership as follows: The goal is to give creatives more opportunities to work on Windows.
The optimized Pro apps are good news for RTX Spark buyers, but they come as no surprise.
Adobe and Nvidia had already announced they were working on this back in the summer, and the first updates followed in October.
I find the integration of Adobe Express into Microsoft Photos more exciting.
This brings Adobe AI into an app that comes pre-installed on virtually every Windows 11 computer.
For Adobe, this is a huge showcase; for users, in the best-case scenario, it’s a convenient way to take better photos without switching programs.
Whether this will actually be practical in the end depends on two questions that Adobe hasn’t answered yet: how much it will cost and how intrusive the link to Express will be.
If every other edit ends with a subscription prompt, the integration will quickly turn into an ad space.
The Insider Preview in December will show which direction things are heading.
